root_cause.text: The PPPoE driver does not reject frames with a compressed (1-byte) protocol field (PFC), and the generic PPP layer (ppp_input()) processes them without negotiated support, causing a one-byte shift in the PPP payload and subsequent 4-byte misalignment of the network header.
root_cause.evidence: The CVE description states that receiving a compressed protocol field "causes the network header to be 4-byte misaligned, which may trigger unaligned access exceptions." The patch adds a check `if (ppp_skb_is_compressed_proto(skb)) goto drop;` in `pppoe_rcv()` to explicitly drop such frames, and introduces the helper `ppp_skb_is_compressed_proto()` to detect compression. The fix also modifies `__ppp_decompress_proto()` to use the same helper.

vuln_statements.explanation: This condition triggers protocol field decompression based solely on the low bit of the first byte, without verifying that Protocol Field Compression (PFC) was negotiated. This allows a one-byte shift for non-negotiated compressed frames, leading to payload misalignment.

This statement unconditionally prepends a zero byte to the packet when the low bit is set, shifting the PPP payload by one byte. This causes a 4-byte misalignment of the network header, which may lead to incorrect packet processing and potential security issues.

This function implements protocol decompression but lacks any check for whether PFC was negotiated. Its very existence as an unconditional decompression routine enables the vulnerability when called on non-negotiated compressed frames.
The opening brace of the vulnerable decompression function. It is part of the code block that executes the vulnerable logic without proper negotiation verification.
The closing brace of the vulnerable function. The function ends without any check to ensure that protocol field compression was actually negotiated, leaving the unconditional decompression in place.

This check is used to identify PPP control protocols (e.g., LCP, IPCP) but does not account for a compressed protocol field. When the protocol field is compressed (1-byte), the host byte order and bit pattern can cause misidentification, contributing to the failure to reject frames with non-negotiated compression.
